---
title: "State space and time-varying parameter models"
subtitle: "Lecture 8"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can stop assuming that a coefficient estimated last
week still holds this week, and instead carry a belief about it forward through time,
updating it by exactly as much as each new observation warrants.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For a linear Gaussian state space model, an unobserved state $\alpha_t$ that evolves
by $\alpha_{t+1} = T_t\alpha_t + R_t\eta_t$ and is measured through
$y_t = Z_t\alpha_t + \varepsilon_t$, the distribution of the state given the data seen
so far is produced by a single recursive update,

$$
a_{t\mid t} = a_{t\mid t-1} + K_t\big(y_t - Z_t a_{t\mid t-1}\big),
\qquad K_t = P_{t\mid t-1}Z_t^\top F_t^{-1},
$$

so today's belief is yesterday's forecast plus a gain times the surprise it did not
predict. The difficulty is that the gain requires an entire covariance matrix to be
carried forward through time rather than a single number, and the same recursion, run
backward instead of forward, is what lets an entire latent history be drawn from its
posterior rather than merely summarised at each date.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. diagnose why a coefficient estimated once and held fixed cannot represent a
   relationship that genuinely drifts, and recognise the symptom in the residuals;
2. derive the Kalman filter recursions from the conditional Normal distribution, and
   the model's log-likelihood as a by-product of the same recursion;
3. derive the forward-filtering backward-sampling recursion that turns the filter into
   a block of a Gibbs sampler;
4. implement the filter and the sampler in Python and apply both to a market beta that
   is allowed to move;
5. compare filtered, smoothed and rolling-window estimates of the same coefficient
   path and say what each can and cannot claim to know;
6. interpret a posterior probability attached to a change in the path, rather than
   only a point estimate at a single date.

Week 8 of 15, paired with the [Week 8 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/08-state-space-tvp.qmd). The chapter assumes the Normal
linear regression posterior of Lecture 2 and the Gibbs sampling logic of Lecture 4;
the Minnesota-prior shrinkage of Lecture 6 is not needed, because nothing here is
solved by regularising a single fixed coefficient.

## Motivation: a beta that will not sit still {#sec-motivation}

Every regression since Lecture 2 has estimated one coefficient and held it fixed for
the whole sample. That is a strong claim whenever the relationship being measured is
itself a claim about behaviour that plausibly changes, and the market beta of a bank
is the cleanest case there is. A bank's equity is a levered claim on its assets, so
standard capital-structure arithmetic says its beta should rise whenever asset values
fall towards the value of its debt, exactly the mechanism that was live throughout
2008. A single beta estimated over decades of data, of the kind Lecture 2 would
produce, averages over any such episode rather than describing it.

**Reading the computation.** The full-sample regression is the benchmark; the three
windows are chosen around three well-documented episodes in the history of the US
banking sector, and none of the three subsample fits uses information from outside
its own window.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
ff_m = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
ind49 = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_industry49_monthly.parquet")

bank = pd.DataFrame({
    "excess": 100.0 * (ind49["banks"] - ff_m["rf"]),   # banks in excess of the bill rate
    "market": 100.0 * ff_m["mkt_rf"],                  # market excess return
}).loc["1970-01-01":].dropna()
bk_y = bank["excess"].to_numpy()
bk_X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(bank)), bank["market"].to_numpy()])
bk_dates = bank.index

b_full = np.linalg.lstsq(bk_X, bk_y, rcond=None)[0]
windows = [("1988-01", "1992-12", "S&L crisis, 1988-1992", "C0"),
           ("1998-01", "2002-12", "dot-com years, 1998-2002", "C1"),
           ("2007-01", "2009-12", "banking crisis, 2007-2009", "C3")]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(bank["market"], bank["excess"], s=6, color="grey", alpha=0.25,
           label="all months")
grid_m = np.linspace(bank["market"].min(), bank["market"].max(), 50)
ax.plot(grid_m, b_full[0] + b_full[1] * grid_m, "k--", lw=1.5,
        label=f"full sample, beta {b_full[1]:.2f}")
for lo, hi, label, col in windows:
    m = (bk_dates >= lo) & (bk_dates <= hi)
    b = np.linalg.lstsq(bk_X[m], bk_y[m], rcond=None)[0]
    ax.plot(grid_m, b[0] + b[1] * grid_m, color=col, lw=2.0,
            label=f"{label}, beta {b[1]:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("market excess return (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("bank excess return (%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8); ax.set_title("One regression line does not fit every era")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{len(bank)} months, {bk_dates[0]:%Y-%m} to {bk_dates[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"full-sample OLS beta {b_full[1]:.4f}")
for lo, hi, label, _ in windows:
    m = (bk_dates >= lo) & (bk_dates <= hi)
    b = np.linalg.lstsq(bk_X[m], bk_y[m], rcond=None)[0]
    print(f"{label}: {m.sum()} months, beta {b[1]:.4f}")
```

Six hundred and seventy-nine months of data give a single OLS beta of $1.0751$. Fitted
separately, the three windows give $1.4411$ at the height of the savings-and-loan
crisis, $0.7573$ at the dot-com peak, and $1.3124$ during 2007 to 2009, a range of
nearly $0.7$ around a full-sample figure that hides all three episodes equally. The
gap between $0.76$ and $1.44$ is not sampling noise from short windows; it is the
levered-equity mechanism showing up exactly where the theory says it should, in the
years the market's own variance was dominated by a sector other than banks and in the
years bank solvency itself was in question.

Two responses are available and both are worse than they look. Refitting a fresh OLS
regression on every five-year window, the informal version of what the picture just
did, throws away every observation outside that window and produces an estimate that
jumps whenever the window moves, with no way to say how much of the jump is signal and
how much is the small-sample noise of sixty months. Reporting the full-sample beta
instead is precise but wrong for any particular date: an investor pricing bank risk in
March 2009 using $1.0751$ is using a number that describes 1970 through 2026 evenly,
not the month in which it is needed. Neither response treats beta as something that
moves gradually and is estimated with more or less confidence depending on how much
has been learned about it so far, which is exactly the gap this chapter closes.

## The problem: a constant coefficient cannot see a drifting one {#sec-problem}

### Result R-8.1: the constant model is a boundary of the general one, and its residuals absorb what it cannot track

Every model in this chapter, including the constant-coefficient regression, is a
special case of the state space form introduced formally in the next section,

$$
y_t = x_t^\top \beta_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim N(0, H),
\qquad \beta_t = \beta_{t-1} + \eta_t, \qquad \eta_t \sim N(0, Q),
$$

with the constant-coefficient regression recovered exactly at $Q = 0$: no state
noise means $\beta_t = \beta_0$ for every $t$, which is the single fixed coefficient
Lecture 2 estimates by least squares. Because $Q = 0$ is a feasible point inside the
larger parameter space rather than a different model, the log-likelihood that this
chapter's filter delivers, maximised freely over $Q \succeq 0$, can never fall below
the log-likelihood at $Q = 0$, for any sample size, any number of coefficients and any
design: $\ell(\hat Q) \ge \ell(0)$ always. A constant model can tie the time-varying
one only when the data show no evidence of drift; it cannot beat it.

What a constant fit reports as measurement noise is correspondingly not a clean
estimate of $H$ whenever $Q > 0$ in truth. Writing $\bar\beta$ for the fixed value a
constant fit converges to and $b_t = \beta_t - \bar\beta$ for how far the true
coefficient has wandered from it at date $t$, the residual of the constant fit is
$e_t = y_t - x_t^\top\bar\beta = x_t^\top b_t + \varepsilon_t$: part genuine noise, part
the piece of a moving coefficient that a single fixed number cannot express. A
regression that looks well fitted by its residual variance alone may simply be
quoting an inflated noise figure for what is, in part, a signal it has thrown away.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The nesting claim is immediate once the state space filter of R-8.2 is available: setting
$Q = 0$ in the transition equation gives $\alpha_{t+1} = T_t\alpha_t$ with no added
randomness, and for the random-walk case used throughout this chapter, $T_t = I$, so
$\alpha_{t+1} = \alpha_t$ with probability one. A state that never moves and is
observed through $y_t = Z_t\alpha_t + \varepsilon_t$ is exactly the classical regression
model of Lecture 2 with $Z_t = x_t^\top$, and it is a textbook fact that the Kalman
filter reduces, in this special case, to recursive least squares: starting from a
diffuse prior, $a_{T\mid T}$ after processing all $T$ observations equals the ordinary
least squares estimate on the whole sample. The log-likelihood the filter reports at
$Q = 0$ is therefore the ordinary Normal regression log-likelihood. Since $Q = 0$ lies
inside the feasible set $Q \succeq 0$ over which the general model's likelihood is
maximised, the maximum over the larger set cannot be smaller than the value already
achieved at one particular feasible point, which is the inequality $\ell(\hat Q) \ge
\ell(0)$.

For the residual decomposition, write the constant fit's probability limit as $\bar\beta$
and note that $b_t = \beta_t - \bar\beta$ inherits the random walk's dependence
structure, $b_{t+1} = b_t + \eta_{t+1}$, so consecutive deviations are strongly
positively correlated whenever $Q$ is small relative to how far the path has already
wandered. The constant fit's residual is $e_t = x_t^\top b_t + \varepsilon_t$, a sum of
a genuinely autocorrelated term and an independent one, so its variance
$\operatorname{Var}(e_t) = x_t^\top\operatorname{Var}(b_t)x_t + H$ is not the constant $H$
the model assumes, and its correlation structure carries the fingerprint of the
coefficient's own path rather than pure measurement noise. Two symptoms follow directly
and can be checked without any further theory: the residual variance is not stable
across sub-periods, since $\operatorname{Var}(b_t)$ is largest exactly when the true
path is farthest from $\bar\beta$, and the squared residuals are serially correlated,
since squaring keeps the sign information in $x_t^\top b_t$ that a single average level
cannot remove.
:::

Both symptoms are checked directly on the constant fit's own residuals from the
bank data already used above.

**Reading the computation.** `resid` is the same full-sample constant-beta residual
computed in the motivation section. The rolling variance uses a five-year window so
that it can be compared with the same crisis and calm episodes already highlighted.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ols-residual-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Rolling five-year variance of the constant-beta residual, and its lag-one autocorrelation in levels against in squares."
bk_resid = bk_y - bk_X @ b_full
roll_var = pd.Series(bk_resid).rolling(60).var()
ac1_level = np.corrcoef(bk_resid[1:], bk_resid[:-1])[0, 1]
ac1_sq = np.corrcoef(bk_resid[1:] ** 2, bk_resid[:-1] ** 2)[0, 1]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.0))
ax.plot(bk_dates, roll_var, color="C3", lw=1.3)
for lo, hi, label, col in windows:
    ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp(lo), pd.Timestamp(hi), color=col, alpha=0.15)
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("rolling 5-year residual variance")
ax.set_title("The constant fit's own residual variance is not constant")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

m_calm = (bk_dates >= "1995-01") & (bk_dates <= "2005-12")
m_crisis = (bk_dates >= "2007-01") & (bk_dates <= "2009-12")
print(f"residual variance, calm 1995-2005: {bk_resid[m_calm].var():.2f}; "
      f"crisis 2007-2009: {bk_resid[m_crisis].var():.2f}")
print(f"lag-1 autocorrelation: residuals {ac1_level:.3f}, squared residuals {ac1_sq:.3f}")
```

The constant fit's residual variance is $16.63$ in the calm decade 1995 to 2005 and
$44.03$ during the 2007 to 2009 crisis, nearly three times as large, exactly the
pattern R-8.1 predicts if beta genuinely moved rather than the noise variance
genuinely tripling, and the rolling-variance line rises and falls in step with the
shaded episodes rather than drifting smoothly. The raw residuals show almost no
serial correlation, a first-lag correlation of $0.015$, because $\bar\beta$ was chosen
precisely to make the mean residual small at every date; but the squared residuals
correlate at $0.261$ from one month to the next, the signature of a variance that
clusters in time because a piece of the true relationship is missing from the model
rather than because volatility itself is truly constant. Least squares is not wrong
about anything it was asked to estimate. It was asked to estimate one number for
sixty years, and the data contain more than one number to find.

## Methodology: the state space model and its two samplers {#sec-methodology}

The repair keeps the two-equation structure already used informally above and makes
it exact. A linear Gaussian **state space model** pairs a **measurement equation**
linking an observed series to a latent **state**, with a **transition equation**
describing how that state evolves,

$$
y_t = Z_t\,\alpha_t + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim N(0, H_t), \qquad\qquad
\alpha_{t+1} = T_t\,\alpha_t + R_t\,\eta_t, \quad \eta_t \sim N(0, Q_t),
$$

with the two shocks independent of each other and over time. The matrices
$Z_t, T_t, R_t, H_t, Q_t$ are the system matrices, often constant across $t$; the
template nests the local level model, the time-varying regression of the previous
section with $Z_t = x_t^\top$, and, stacked appropriately, the time-varying vector
autoregression of Primiceri (2005), in which both the autoregressive coefficients and
the shock covariance of a macroeconomic system are allowed to drift, a model credited
with much of what is known about how the transmission of monetary policy changed
across the post-war period.

### Result R-8.2: the Kalman filter recursions, and the likelihood as a by-product

Suppose $\alpha_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(a_{t\mid t-1}, P_{t\mid t-1})$. Then the
distribution of the state given data up to and including date $t$ is again exactly
Normal, and is produced by

$$
v_t = y_t - Z_t a_{t\mid t-1}, \qquad F_t = Z_tP_{t\mid t-1}Z_t^\top + H_t, \qquad
K_t = P_{t\mid t-1}Z_t^\top F_t^{-1},
$$
$$
a_{t\mid t} = a_{t\mid t-1} + K_t v_t, \qquad P_{t\mid t} = (I - K_tZ_t)P_{t\mid t-1},
\qquad\qquad
a_{t+1\mid t} = T_t a_{t\mid t}, \qquad P_{t+1\mid t} = T_tP_{t\mid t}T_t^\top + R_tQ_tR_t^\top,
$$

for any sample size, any state dimension, and any sequence of system matrices. The
same recursion delivers the model's log-likelihood at no extra cost, because the
chain rule factors the joint density of the data into one-step-ahead predictive
factors with no assumption beyond the model already written down,
$p(y_{1:T}) = \prod_t p(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$, and each factor is available in closed
form as the Normal density of $v_t$ with variance $F_t$: $\log p(y_{1:T}) =
-\tfrac12\sum_t\big(\log 2\pi + \log F_t + v_t^2/F_t\big)$ in the scalar case, with the
obvious matrix generalisation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Since $\alpha_t \mid y_{1:t-1}$ is Normal and $y_t = Z_t\alpha_t + \varepsilon_t$ is an
affine function of it plus independent Normal noise, the pair $(\alpha_t, y_t)$ is
jointly Normal given $y_{1:t-1}$. Its mean is $(a_{t\mid t-1}, Z_ta_{t\mid t-1})$ since
$\varepsilon_t$ has mean zero; its state variance is $P_{t\mid t-1}$; its observation
variance is $Z_tP_{t\mid t-1}Z_t^\top + H_t \equiv F_t$, the two pieces adding because
$\varepsilon_t$ is independent of $\alpha_t$; and the cross covariance is
$\operatorname{Cov}(\alpha_t,y_t) = P_{t\mid t-1}Z_t^\top$, again because the
$\varepsilon_t$ cross term vanishes. Applying the conditional Normal formula to this
joint distribution, with $\alpha_t$ playing the role of the unobserved coordinate and
$y_t$ the observed one, gives exactly the displayed $a_{t\mid t}$ and $P_{t\mid t}$,
with $K_t = P_{t\mid t-1}Z_t^\top F_t^{-1}$ read literally as a covariance divided by a
variance, the population regression coefficient of the state on the observed surprise.
The prediction step then applies the transition equation to this updated
distribution: taking expectations through the linear map $T_t$ gives $a_{t+1\mid t} =
T_ta_{t\mid t}$, and taking variances, using the independence of $\eta_t$ from
everything dated $t$ or earlier, gives $P_{t+1\mid t} = T_tP_{t\mid t}T_t^\top +
R_tQ_tR_t^\top$. Conditioning on data always subtracts from the variance; letting the
state evolve always adds to it, and the filter is that alternation, repeated once per
date.

For the likelihood, the chain rule for densities factorises the joint density of any
sequence of random variables into one-step conditionals with no assumption whatsoever,
$p(y_{1:T}) = \prod_{t=1}^T p(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1})$, turning a $T$-dimensional
integral over the whole latent path into a product of $T$ one-dimensional predictive
densities. Each factor is exactly the Normal density of $v_t = y_t - Z_ta_{t\mid t-1}$
with variance $F_t$, both of which the filter has already computed on its way past, so
summing $\log N(v_t; 0, F_t)$ over $t$ recovers $\log p(y_{1:T})$ with no further
integration required. Because $\theta$ here is only the variances $H$ and $Q$, this
expression can be maximised, or compared across candidate values, exactly as a
likelihood is used anywhere else in this course, and a gap of $\lambda$ log points
between two settings is a log Bayes factor of $\lambda$ in favour of one over the
other.
:::

### Result R-8.3: forward-filtering, backward-sampling

A full Bayesian treatment does not want a single filtered path; it wants draws of the
entire latent sequence from its posterior, so that the variances $H$ and $Q$ can in
turn be updated conditional on a sampled path inside a Gibbs sampler. Given the
variances, a draw of the whole path $\alpha_{1:T}$ from $p(\alpha_{1:T} \mid y_{1:T})$
is obtained by running the filter above once, then drawing $\alpha_T \sim
N(a_{T\mid T}, P_{T\mid T})$ and, for $t = T-1$ down to $1$,

$$
\alpha_t \mid \alpha_{t+1}, y_{1:t} \sim N\!\Big(a_{t\mid t} + J_t\big(\alpha_{t+1} -
T_t a_{t\mid t}\big),\;\; P_{t\mid t} - J_tP_{t+1\mid t}J_t^\top\Big),
\qquad J_t = P_{t\mid t}T_t^\top P_{t+1\mid t}^{-1},
$$

for any linear Gaussian state space model, at a cost linear in $T$: one forward pass
plus one small Normal draw per date.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Write the joint posterior of the path backwards using the chain rule, an identity
rather than an assumption, $p(\alpha_{1:T}\mid y_{1:T}) = p(\alpha_T \mid y_{1:T})
\prod_{t=1}^{T-1} p(\alpha_t \mid \alpha_{t+1:T}, y_{1:T})$. Two conditional
independencies simplify the generic factor. First, the state is Markov, so given
$\alpha_{t+1}$ the later states carry no further information about $\alpha_t$. Second,
every later observation $y_s$, $s > t$, depends on the path only through $\alpha_s$,
and every such $\alpha_s$ depends on $\alpha_t$ only through $\alpha_{t+1}$, so once
$\alpha_{t+1}$ is fixed the future of the system is cut off from $\alpha_t$. Together
these give $p(\alpha_t \mid \alpha_{t+1:T}, y_{1:T}) = p(\alpha_t \mid \alpha_{t+1},
y_{1:t})$, a density that involves only quantities the forward filter has already
produced, which is what makes the backward sweep cheap: it never touches the data
again.

By Bayes' theorem, $p(\alpha_t \mid \alpha_{t+1}, y_{1:t}) \propto p(\alpha_{t+1} \mid
\alpha_t)\,p(\alpha_t \mid y_{1:t})$. The second factor is the filtered posterior
$N(a_{t\mid t}, P_{t\mid t})$; the first, viewed as a function of $\alpha_t$, is a
Normal likelihood with the already-sampled $\alpha_{t+1}$ playing the role of an extra
observation, transition matrix $T_t$ and noise covariance $R_tQ_tR_t^\top$. This is
therefore one more instance of the update in R-8.2, with $\alpha_{t+1}$ as data, $T_t$
as the observation matrix and $R_tQ_tR_t^\top$ as the measurement variance. Writing
$P_{t+1\mid t} = T_tP_{t\mid t}T_t^\top + R_tQ_tR_t^\top$ for the variance of this
pseudo-observation, the same substitution that produced $K_t$ now produces $J_t =
P_{t\mid t}T_t^\top P_{t+1\mid t}^{-1}$, and the displayed conditional follows exactly
as $a_{t\mid t}$ and $P_{t\mid t}$ did before.

The mean of many draws from this recursion converges to the smoother's $a_{t\mid T}$,
so the classical Kalman smoother is recoverable from this sampler but not the reverse:
nothing in a collection of smoothed marginal means and variances records the posterior
correlation between $\alpha_t$ and $\alpha_{t+1}$, which is exactly what makes a single
sampled path wiggle coherently through time instead of behaving like independent draws
from separate pointwise bands, and exactly what a Gibbs sampler needs in order to
update the variances conditional on a specific, internally consistent path.
:::

The two results compose into the sampler this chapter uses on real data. Given the
current variances, R-8.3 draws a whole path; given that path, the measurement
residuals and the state increments are the sum of squares of two independent
regressions with known regressors, so under the course's conjugate prior
$\sigma^2 \sim IG(\alpha_0, \delta_0)$ the variances have standard inverse-gamma
conditional posteriors and are drawn in turn. Iterating the two steps is a Gibbs
sampler whose every draw is a complete, internally consistent history of the
coefficient together with a value for how fast it is allowed to move.

## Data: the market beta of US banks, 1970 to 2026 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the same one introduced in the motivation: the monthly
value-weighted return of the Fama-French 49 bank industry portfolio and the
Fama-French market factor, both from `ff_industry49_monthly.parquet` and
`ff_factors_monthly.parquet`. Both are converted to excess-of-bill-rate returns in
percentage points and no other series is used anywhere in this chapter. Banks are the
right sector for this question for three reasons already used above: their equity is
a levered claim whose beta should mechanically move with asset values, they were the
epicentre rather than a bystander of the 2008 crisis, and the industry has a long
enough documented history, from the savings-and-loan crisis through the pandemic
shock, to give a time-varying model several independent chances to be right or wrong.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bank-market-series
#| fig-cap: "Monthly excess returns on the US banking sector and the market, 1970 to 2026. The shaded bands mark the three episodes used earlier in this chapter."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.0))
ax.plot(bk_dates, bank["excess"], color="C3", lw=0.6, alpha=0.85, label="banks")
ax.plot(bk_dates, bank["market"], color="steelblue", lw=0.6, alpha=0.6, label="market")
for lo, hi, _, col in windows:
    ax.axvspan(pd.Timestamp(lo), pd.Timestamp(hi), color=col, alpha=0.12)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("excess return (%)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("US bank and market excess returns, 1970 to 2026")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(bank.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3).to_string())
print(f"correlation of bank and market excess returns: {bank['excess'].corr(bank['market']):.3f}")
```

Bank excess returns average $0.659$ percent a month against the market's $0.625$, with
a standard deviation of $6.177$ against the market's $4.575$: banks earn a slightly
higher raw return but carry so much more risk that their risk-adjusted compensation,
mean divided by standard deviation, is noticeably lower than the market's. The two
series correlate at $0.796$, confirming that a single-factor market model is a
reasonable starting point, and the shaded bands mark exactly the
three episodes already shown to carry different betas. Bank returns are visibly more
volatile inside the crisis band than elsewhere in the picture, which is the same
symptom identified in R-8.1 appearing in the raw data before any model is fitted to
it.

## Empirical analysis: filtering, smoothing and sampling a drifting beta {#sec-empirical}

The state space model for this dataset lets alpha and beta drift together,
$s_t = (\alpha_t,\beta_t)^\top$, $s_t = s_{t-1} + \eta_t$, observed through
$r_{b,t} - r_{f,t} = x_t^\top s_t + \varepsilon_t$ with $x_t = (1, r_{m,t}-r_{f,t})^\top$,
exactly the general form of R-8.2 with $Z_t = x_t^\top$ and $T_t = R_t = I_2$. We
parameterise the state variance in signal-to-noise form, $Q = H\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_\alpha,
\lambda_\beta)$, fix $H$ at the constant-fit residual variance as a starting value, and
choose the two ratios by the marginal likelihood R-8.2 provides.

```{python}
def kalman_tvp(y, X, H, Q, P1=100.0, smooth=True):
    n_t, k = X.shape
    a = np.zeros(k); P = np.eye(k) * P1
    a_f = np.empty((n_t, k)); P_f = np.empty((n_t, k, k))
    a_p = np.empty((n_t, k)); P_p = np.empty((n_t, k, k))
    v = np.empty(n_t); F = np.empty(n_t); loglik = 0.0
    for t in range(n_t):
        a_p[t], P_p[t] = a, P
        x = X[t]; Px = P @ x
        v[t] = y[t] - x @ a
        F[t] = x @ Px + H
        K = Px / F[t]
        a = a + K * v[t]
        P = P - np.outer(K, Px)
        a_f[t], P_f[t] = a, P
        loglik += -0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(F[t]) + v[t] ** 2 / F[t])
        P = P + Q
    out = dict(a_f=a_f, P_f=P_f, a_p=a_p, P_p=P_p, v=v, F=F, loglik=loglik)
    if smooth:
        a_s = a_f.copy(); P_s = P_f.copy()
        for t in range(n_t - 2, -1, -1):
            J = P_f[t] @ np.linalg.inv(P_p[t + 1])
            a_s[t] = a_f[t] + J @ (a_s[t + 1] - a_p[t + 1])
            P_s[t] = P_f[t] + J @ (P_s[t + 1] - P_p[t + 1]) @ J.T
        out["a_s"], out["P_s"] = a_s, P_s
    return out

bk_resid = bk_y - bk_X @ b_full
bk_H = bk_resid @ bk_resid / (len(bk_y) - 2)

lam_grid = np.logspace(-6, -1.5, 46)
ll_grid = np.array([[kalman_tvp(bk_y, bk_X, bk_H, bk_H * np.diag([la, lb]),
                                smooth=False)["loglik"] for lb in lam_grid]
                    for la in lam_grid])
i_a, i_b = np.unravel_index(ll_grid.argmax(), ll_grid.shape)
lam_a, lam_b = lam_grid[i_a], lam_grid[i_b]
ll_const = kalman_tvp(bk_y, bk_X, bk_H, bk_H * np.diag([1e-8, 1e-8]),
                      smooth=False)["loglik"]

print(f"best lambda_alpha {lam_a:.2e}, best lambda_beta {lam_b:.2e}")
print(f"log marginal likelihood: time-varying {ll_grid.max():.2f}, "
      f"constant coefficients {ll_const:.2f}, difference {ll_grid.max() - ll_const:.2f}")
print(f"implied sd of the monthly innovation to beta: {np.sqrt(bk_H * lam_b):.4f}")
```

The grid puts $\lambda_\alpha$ at its lower bound, so the data see no evidence of a
drifting alpha: an industry portfolio's abnormal return is close to zero and stays
there. Beta is different. The preferred $\lambda_\beta = 2.51\times10^{-4}$ implies a
monthly innovation standard deviation of $0.0593$, so beta can plausibly move by about
$0.2$ over a year, and the log marginal likelihood rises by $12.11$ points over the
constant-coefficient model, exactly R-8.1's inequality with the gap now measured: a
log Bayes factor of twelve is decisive evidence on any of the usual scales.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tvp-filtered-smoothed
#| fig-cap: "Filtered and smoothed estimates of the banks portfolio's market beta, at the marginal-likelihood-preferred signal-to-noise ratio. The dashed line is the full-sample constant-beta estimate."
bk = kalman_tvp(bk_y, bk_X, bk_H, bk_H * np.diag([lam_a, lam_b]))
beta_f, beta_s = bk["a_f"][:, 1], bk["a_s"][:, 1]
sd_f = np.sqrt(bk["P_f"][:, 1, 1]); sd_s = np.sqrt(bk["P_s"][:, 1, 1])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.2))
ax.fill_between(bk_dates, beta_s - 1.96 * sd_s, beta_s + 1.96 * sd_s,
                color="C3", alpha=0.18, label="95% smoothed band")
ax.plot(bk_dates, beta_f, color="C0", lw=1.0, label=r"filtered $\beta_{t|t}$")
ax.plot(bk_dates, beta_s, color="C3", lw=1.8, label=r"smoothed $\beta_{t|T}$")
ax.axhline(b_full[1], color="black", ls="--", lw=1.0, label=f"constant OLS beta {b_full[1]:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("market beta of banks")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left", ncol=2)
ax.set_title("The market beta of US banks is not a constant")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for lab in ["1991-01", "2000-06", "2006-12", "2008-09", "2009-03", "2020-03"]:
    t = bk_dates.get_loc(pd.Timestamp(lab + "-01"))
    print(f"{lab}: filtered {beta_f[t]:.3f} (sd {sd_f[t]:.3f}), smoothed {beta_s[t]:.3f} (sd {sd_s[t]:.3f})")
print(f"smoothed beta ranges from {beta_s.min():.3f} to {beta_s.max():.3f}")
print(f"mean filtered sd {sd_f.mean():.4f}, mean smoothed sd {sd_s.mean():.4f}")
```

The smoothed path recovers, from the data alone, exactly the three episodes the
motivation used to make its case: a peak of $1.484$ in January 1991 during the
savings-and-loan crisis, a trough of $0.526$ at the June 2000 dot-com peak, and a
climb to $1.392$ by March 2009, the month the market bottomed. Averaged over the whole
sample the smoothed standard deviation is $0.1644$ against the filtered $0.2326$, a
thirty percent reduction: knowing what happened afterwards sharpens every historical
estimate, because the smoother conditions on the whole sample rather than only the
past.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tvp-rolling
#| fig-cap: "Sixty-month rolling-window OLS beta against the smoothed state space estimate."
win = 60
roll_beta = np.full(len(bk_y), np.nan)
for t in range(win - 1, len(bk_y)):
    Xw, yw = bk_X[t - win + 1:t + 1], bk_y[t - win + 1:t + 1]
    roll_beta[t] = np.linalg.lstsq(Xw, yw, rcond=None)[0][1]
ok = ~np.isnan(roll_beta)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.2))
ax.plot(bk_dates, roll_beta, color="C1", lw=1.2, label="60-month rolling OLS")
ax.plot(bk_dates, beta_s, color="C3", lw=1.8, label="smoothed state space")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("market beta")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
ax.set_title("A cruder filter against the state space estimate")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"correlation of rolling and smoothed beta: {np.corrcoef(roll_beta[ok], beta_s[ok])[0,1]:.3f}")
print(f"sd of month-to-month changes: rolling {np.std(np.diff(roll_beta[ok])):.4f}, "
      f"smoothed {np.std(np.diff(beta_s)):.4f}")
t0809 = bk_dates.get_loc(pd.Timestamp("2008-09-01"))
print(f"Sept 2008: rolling {roll_beta[t0809]:.3f}, filtered {beta_f[t0809]:.3f}, smoothed {beta_s[t0809]:.3f}")
```

A rolling window is a defensible cruder filter, not a wrong one, and comparing it
against the state space estimate says exactly what it buys. The two series correlate
at only $0.566$, and the rolling line is nearly three times as jumpy, a standard
deviation of month-to-month changes of $0.0309$ against $0.0109$, because a single
large return shifts the window and then, sixty months later, drops back out of it and
shifts the estimate back for no economic reason. It also lags: in September 2008 it
still reads $0.790$, four fifths of its window still the placid mid-2000s, while the
smoothed estimate is already at $1.183$. The rolling window's one advantage is real:
its September 2008 value is close to the *filtered*, real-time estimate of $0.741$,
which is the number an investor could actually have had that month. For describing
history rather than reacting to it in real time, the state space smoother dominates.

```{python}
def ffbs_draw(y, X, H, Q, rng):
    n_t, k = X.shape
    a = np.zeros(k); P = np.eye(k) * 100.0
    a_f = np.empty((n_t, k)); P_f = np.empty((n_t, k, k))
    for t in range(n_t):
        x = X[t]; Px = P @ x
        F = x @ Px + H; K = Px / F
        a = a + K * (y[t] - x @ a); P = P - np.outer(K, Px)
        a_f[t], P_f[t] = a, P
        P = P + Q
    s = np.empty((n_t, k)); z = rng.standard_normal((n_t, k))
    s[-1] = a_f[-1] + np.linalg.cholesky(P_f[-1]) @ z[-1]
    for t in range(n_t - 2, -1, -1):
        Pf = P_f[t]; Ppred = Pf + Q
        J = np.linalg.solve(Ppred.T, Pf.T).T
        C = Pf - J @ Ppred @ J.T
        s[t] = a_f[t] + J @ (s[t + 1] - a_f[t]) + np.linalg.cholesky((C + C.T) / 2) @ z[t]
    return s

def gibbs_tvp(y, X, rng, alpha_q=3.0, delta_q=1e-3, n_iter=1000, burn=200):
    n_t, k = X.shape
    alpha_0, delta_0 = 3.0, 2.0
    H, lam = bk_H, 2.5e-4
    beta_draws = np.empty((n_iter - burn, n_t)); par = np.empty((n_iter - burn, 2))
    for it in range(n_iter):
        s = ffbs_draw(y, X, H, H * lam * np.eye(k), rng)
        resid = y - np.einsum("tk,tk->t", X, s)
        ssq = np.sum(np.diff(s, axis=0) ** 2)
        H = stats.invgamma.rvs(a=alpha_0 + n_t / 2 + k * (n_t - 1) / 2,
                               scale=delta_0 + 0.5 * resid @ resid + 0.5 * ssq / lam,
                               random_state=rng)
        lam = stats.invgamma.rvs(a=alpha_q + k * (n_t - 1) / 2,
                                 scale=delta_q + 0.5 * ssq / H, random_state=rng)
        if it >= burn:
            beta_draws[it - burn] = s[:, 1]; par[it - burn] = (H, lam)
    return beta_draws, par

B_draws, gib_par = gibbs_tvp(bk_y, bk_X, np.random.default_rng(88))
print(f"{B_draws.shape[0]} retained sweeps")
print(f"lambda: median {np.median(gib_par[:,1]):.3e}, "
      f"90% interval [{np.quantile(gib_par[:,1],0.05):.3e}, {np.quantile(gib_par[:,1],0.95):.3e}]")
print(f"mean posterior sd of beta: Gibbs {B_draws.std(axis=0, ddof=1).mean():.4f}, "
      f"plug-in smoother {sd_s.mean():.4f}")
```

Everything above conditions on a single plug-in value of the signal-to-noise ratio,
the one that maximised the marginal likelihood. R-8.3's sampler treats it as unknown
instead. The posterior median of $\lambda$ is $4.06\times10^{-4}$, higher than the
plug-in value, with a ninety percent interval spanning a factor of three and a half,
and the sampler's average posterior standard deviation for beta, $0.1831$, exceeds the
plug-in smoother's $0.1644$: part of the width the plug-in version omits is honest
uncertainty about how fast beta drifts at all.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tvp-gibbs
#| fig-cap: "Posterior median and 95% credible band for the beta path from the Gibbs sampler, against the plug-in smoothed path."
lo_g, med_g, hi_g = np.quantile(B_draws, [0.025, 0.5, 0.975], axis=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.2))
ax.fill_between(bk_dates, lo_g, hi_g, color="C4", alpha=0.22, label="95% credible band")
ax.plot(bk_dates, med_g, color="C4", lw=1.8, label="posterior median")
ax.plot(bk_dates, beta_s, color="C3", lw=1.2, ls="--", label="plug-in smoothed")
ax.axhline(b_full[1], color="black", ls=":", lw=1.0)
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("market beta of banks")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower left")
ax.set_title("The posterior beta path, variances integrated out")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

t06 = bk_dates.get_loc(pd.Timestamp("2006-12-01")); t09 = bk_dates.get_loc(pd.Timestamp("2009-03-01"))
t91 = bk_dates.get_loc(pd.Timestamp("1991-01-01")); t00 = bk_dates.get_loc(pd.Timestamp("2000-06-01"))
print(f"P(beta higher in 2009-03 than in 2006-12) = {(B_draws[:,t09] > B_draws[:,t06]).mean():.4f}, "
      f"mean rise {(B_draws[:,t09] - B_draws[:,t06]).mean():.3f}")
print(f"P(beta lower in 2000-06 than in 1991-01) = {(B_draws[:,t00] < B_draws[:,t91]).mean():.4f}")
```

The posterior median tracks the plug-in smoothed path closely, so nothing above is
overturned by admitting uncertainty about the drift rate, but the sampler answers
questions the pointwise bands cannot. The posterior probability that beta was higher
in March 2009 than in December 2006 is $0.9825$, with a posterior mean rise of
$0.565$: the crisis-era increase is a claim the data support with high confidence, not
merely a feature of one point estimate. The probability that beta was lower at the
dot-com peak than at the savings-and-loan peak is $1.0000$, every retained draw
agreeing. Neither statement could be read off the pointwise ninety percent intervals
for those dates, which overlap; the difference between two dates is decisively signed
because the sampler tracks how a whole path moves together, which is precisely what
FFBS was built to preserve.

## Discussion: what the filter buys, and what it cannot tell you {#sec-discussion}

The bank's question was whether a levered sector's exposure to the market moves with
its own solvency, and the filter answers yes, with a path that reproduces three
separate episodes of financial history without being told where to look for them: the
savings-and-loan peak, the dot-com trough, and the 2008 climb all appear at the dates
independent economic history already assigns them. That is the check against
something already known, and it is worth confirming that the log-likelihood advantage
of R-8.1 is not manufactured by one unusual episode.

**Reading the computation.** Each point is the running difference between the
time-varying model's and the constant model's one-step-ahead log predictive density,
using the filtered quantities already computed in @sec-empirical. A steadily rising
line means the advantage accrues throughout the sample; a single jump would mean one
episode was doing all the work.

```{python}
#| label: fig-loglik-gap
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative one-step-ahead log predictive density, time-varying model minus constant-coefficient model."
r_tv = kalman_tvp(bk_y, bk_X, bk_H, bk_H * np.diag([lam_a, lam_b]), smooth=False)
r_c = kalman_tvp(bk_y, bk_X, bk_H, bk_H * np.diag([1e-8, 1e-8]), smooth=False)
v_tv, F_tv, v_c, F_c = r_tv["v"], r_tv["F"], r_c["v"], r_c["F"]
ll_tv = -0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(F_tv) + v_tv ** 2 / F_tv)
ll_c = -0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(F_c) + v_c ** 2 / F_c)
gap = np.cumsum(ll_tv - ll_c)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 3.8))
ax.plot(bk_dates, gap, color="C0", lw=1.4)
ax.axhline(0.0, color="black", lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.set_xlabel("date"); ax.set_ylabel("cumulative log-likelihood gap")
ax.set_title("The time-varying model's advantage accrues throughout the sample")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"cumulative gap at end of sample: {gap[-1]:.2f}; "
      f"gap contributed by the 2007-2009 crisis alone: {(ll_tv-ll_c)[m_crisis].sum():.2f}")
```

The line climbs unevenly but never reverses for long, and only $3.50$ of the final
$12.11$ log points come from the 2007 to 2009 crisis itself, about a quarter of the
total. A
model built purely to track a number, with no reference to levered-equity theory or
banking history, has recovered the qualitative shape of the theory anyway across many
separate episodes rather than one, which is good evidence that the state space
specification, and not merely a single dramatic period, is doing the work.

It is also worth being honest about a choice buried inside this chapter's own method.
Both the marginal-likelihood plug-in and the Gibbs sampler settled on one number,
$\lambda_\beta \approx 2.5$ to $4\times10^{-4}$, as the state's signal-to-noise ratio,
and everything reported above conditions on that choice being the right specification
for how beta moves. R-8.1 showed that a constant model cannot beat a time-varying one
because it is a nested special case; but nothing said the reverse, that the particular
time-varying specification maximising the marginal likelihood among many candidates
is the one to trust going forward. Picking the single best-supported specification and
proceeding as though it were certainly correct is exactly the same manoeuvre as
picking the single most probable model in a much larger comparison, and it carries the
same risk: a specification chosen because it happened to fit best on this sample can
be an overconfident guide to the next one.

That is the next chapter's subject, in a setting where it is not one nuisance
parameter but the whole specification, predictors and all, that is in question.
Choosing the single best model in sample, exactly as this chapter chose one
signal-to-noise ratio, loses money out of sample whenever the comparison among
candidates is close, and Lecture 9 shows both how badly that can go wrong and what
averaging over the candidates buys instead.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 8 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/08-state-space-tvp.qmd) works through them, adds a lab
built around a time-varying Phillips curve, and revisits the Kalman filter from first
principles on a simulated local-level model.

1. By hand. Starting from R-8.2, set $T_t = R_t = 1$ and $Z_t = 1$ for all $t$ and
   show that the steady-state Kalman gain, the fixed point of $K$ as $t \to \infty$
   with $H$ and $Q$ constant, solves a quadratic equation in $K$ whose only root in
   $[0,1]$ is $K^\ast = \big(-q + \sqrt{q^2+4q}\big)/2$ with $q = Q/H$. Confirm that
   $K^\ast \to 0$ as $q \to 0$ and $K^\ast \to 1$ as $q \to \infty$, and interpret both
   limits in terms of R-8.1.

2. Computational. Refit the bank beta model of @sec-empirical with $\lambda_\alpha$
   fixed at zero rather than chosen by the grid, forcing a constant alpha and a
   drifting beta only, and report how much the log marginal likelihood changes and
   whether the smoothed beta path moves. Then repeat the marginal-likelihood grid
   search with $H$ re-estimated jointly with $Q$ rather than fixed at the constant-fit
   value, and report whether the preferred signal-to-noise ratio changes.

3. On real data. Add the ten-year Treasury yield as a second regressor alongside the
   market factor, refit the three-dimensional state space model of R-8.2, and report
   whether the interest-rate exposure of bank equity is itself time varying and
   whether allowing it to drift changes the beta path recovered in @sec-empirical.

Exercise 1 is worth attempting before the session, since the steady-state gain is used
without derivation in the Phillips-curve lab. Exercises 2 and 3 reuse the code of
@sec-empirical with the state dimension or the prior changed.

## Reading and references

The state space form and the Kalman filter recursions of R-8.2 follow Frühwirth-Schnatter,
*Bayesian Computing*, Part IV, and Greenberg (2008), Section 10.3. The
forward-filtering backward-sampling recursion of R-8.3 follows the same sources and is
the standard reference implementation used across the time-varying-parameter
literature. The time-varying VAR mentioned in the methodology section is Primiceri
(2005). The data are the Fama-French factor and industry portfolio files distributed
with this course as repository snapshots.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly
structure; consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Primiceri (2005), "Time Varying Structural Vector Autoregressions and Monetary Policy,"
*Review of Economic Studies*. Koop, *Bayesian Econometrics*, ch. 8 on state-space
models. Chan, Koop, Poirier, and Tobias, *Bayesian Econometric Methods* (2nd ed.), ch.
on state-space and TVP models. Gelman et al., *Bayesian Data Analysis* (3rd ed.), ch.
18 on hierarchical and dynamic models.
